claim: Over two-thirds of integral membrane proteins of known structure assemble into oligomers.
source: Over two-thirds of integral membrane proteins of known structure assemble into oligomers.
evidence: This is a general statement about membrane protein structures supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Among membrane-protein classes of known structure, approximately 70% are found as homo- or hetero-oligomers.
source: Indeed, among membrane-protein classes of known structure, approximately 70% are found as homo- or hetero-oligomers (Aleksandrova et al., 2020), compared with about 55% of water-soluble proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aleksandrova et al., 2020.

claim: About 55% of water-soluble proteins are found as oligomers.
source: Indeed, among membrane-protein classes of known structure, approximately 70% are found as homo- or hetero-oligomers (Aleksandrova et al., 2020), compared with about 55% of water-soluble proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to membrane proteins and is supported by citation context.

claim: The lipid bilayer interior is a ≈30 Å layer of low-dielectric fluid oil.
source: The bilayer interior, formed by the acyl chains, is a ≈30 Å layer of low-dielectric fluid oil (Fricke, 1925) that provides a natural electrostatic barrier for the passage of charged and polar species.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fricke, 1925.

claim: Cellular membranes include hundreds of lipid types.
source: Lipidomics studies indeed show that cellular membranes include hundreds of lipid types (Brügger, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brügger, 2014.

claim: Under cold growth temperatures E. coli generates unsaturated lipids to increase membrane fluidity.
source: For example, under cold growth temperatures E. coli generates unsaturated lipids to increase membrane fluidity, but it also increases production of short-chain lipids (Marr and Ingraham, 1962; Sanders and Mittendorf, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marr and Ingraham, 1962 and Sanders and Mittendorf, 2011.

claim: Under cold growth temperatures E. coli increases production of short-chain lipids.
source: For example, under cold growth temperatures E. coli generates unsaturated lipids to increase membrane fluidity, but it also increases production of short-chain lipids (Marr and Ingraham, 1962; Sanders and Mittendorf, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marr and Ingraham, 1962 and Sanders and Mittendorf, 2011.

claim: The CLC-ec1 homodimer is a Cl-/H+ antiporter.
source: Integrating experimental and computational approaches, we show that monomers associate to avoid a thinned-membrane defect formed by hydrophobic mismatch at their exposed dimerization interfaces.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and title of the manuscript.

claim: The dimerization interface of CLC-ec1 is about 1200 Å2, most of which is inside the membrane.
source: While CLC-ec1 had been known to exist as a homodimer in detergent and membranes (Maduke et al., 1999; Dutzler et al., 2002), our measurements revealed this complex results from association of two functionally competent monomers (Robertson et al., 2010), via an interface of about 1200 Å2, most of which is inside the membrane (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The measured equilibrium dimerization free energy for CLC-ec1 is −10.9 kcal/mole relative to a standard state of 1 monomer/lipid.
source: Specifically, the measured equilibrium dimerization free energy for this complex is −10.9 kcal/mole, relative to a standard state of 1 monomer/lipid (Chadda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chadda et al., 2018.

claim: The CLC-ec1 monomer in 2:1 POPE/POPG introduces a thinned-membrane defect in the surrounding membrane.
source: Our computational studies demonstrate that the CLC-ec1 monomer in 2:1 POPE/POPG introduces a non-native thinned defect in the surrounding membrane, due to the exposure of the shorter central helices that form the core of the dimerization interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational studies described in the manuscript.

claim: The magnitude of the thinning defect caused by monomeric CLC-ec1 is about 8 Å relative to the bulk.
source: Quantitative analysis of bilayer thickness, measured by the separation between the outer and inner ester layers and represented on a 2D heat map, shows that the magnitude of this thinning defect is about 8 Å relative to the bulk (Figure 2C), that is, nearly a quarter of the unperturbed hydrophobic thickness of this 2:1 POPE/POPG membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The thinning defect represents nearly a quarter of the unperturbed hydrophobic thickness of 2:1 POPE/POPG membrane.
source: Quantitative analysis of bilayer thickness, measured by the separation between the outer and inner ester layers and represented on a 2D heat map, shows that the magnitude of this thinning defect is about 8 Å relative to the bulk (Figure 2C), that is, nearly a quarter of the unperturbed hydrophobic thickness of this 2:1 POPE/POPG membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The membrane thinning defect is specific to the dimerization interface in the monomeric state.
source: This defect is also clearly specific to the dimerization interface in the monomeric state, consistent with the 3D density maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of 3D density maps from simulations.

claim: The mean acyl chain end-to-end distance near the protein is only a fraction of 1 Å smaller than the bulk value.
source: In this case, however, the mean acyl chain end-to-end distance near the protein is only a fraction of 1 Å smaller than the bulk value (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A); this minor perturbation is also not specific to the dimerization interface, but is present at other regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The thinning defect does not arise due to significant compression of the acyl chains.
source: Therefore, the thinning defect that we observe does not arise due to a significant compression of the acyl chains.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of acyl chain end-to-end distances.

claim: Increased lipid-chain tilt is in large part what leads to the membrane thinning.
source: Instead, our simulations show that increased lipid-chain tilt is in large part what leads to the membrane thinning.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data analyzing lipid-chain tilt.

claim: The mean lipid-chain tilt angle is maximally deflected by 60° at the dimerization interface in both leaflets.
source: Approaching the dimerization interface, however, this angle increases gradually and is maximally deflected by 60°, in both leaflets.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid-chain tilt angles from simulations.

claim: Near the dimerization interface the acyl chains in one leaflet show a greater degree of inter-digitation with those in the other leaflet compared to the bulk.
source: Alongside this drastic change in tilt angle, we also observe that near the dimerization interface the acyl chains in one leaflet show a greater degree of inter-digitation with those in the other leaflet (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), compared to the bulk or elsewhere along the protein perimeter.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The perturbations in the membrane are symmetric with respect to the bilayer midplane.
source: Interestingly, the perturbations we observe are in all cases symmetric with respect to the bilayer midplane, consistent with the fact that the CLC-ec1 monomer consists of two topologically inverted structural repeats; this observation further underscores that it is the protein structure that dictates the morphology of the adjacent bilayer.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation observations and structural knowledge of CLC-ec1.

claim: DL lipids are shorter than PO lipids by 4–6 carbons per chain.
source: DL lipids are shorter than PO lipids by 4–6 carbons per chain, and are also fully saturated, losing the ω−9 double bond in one chain.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical structure of the lipids used.

claim: DL lipids are fully saturated, losing the ω−9 double bond in one chain compared to PO lipids.
source: DL lipids are shorter than PO lipids by 4–6 carbons per chain, and are also fully saturated, losing the ω−9 double bond in one chain.
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical structure of the lipids used.

claim: The DL/PO mixtures show broad phase-transition profiles.
source: The mixtures show broad profiles; however, the membranes are fluid at room temperature, with the exception of the 100% DL condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by DSC measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: The membranes are fluid at room temperature, with the exception of the 100% DL condition.
source: The mixtures show broad profiles; however, the membranes are fluid at room temperature, with the exception of the 100% DL condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by DSC measurements described in the manuscript.

claim: The peak Tm as a function of DL shows eutectic behavior with a minimum Tm at about 30% DL.
source: Plotting the peak Tm as a function of DL shows eutectic behavior with a minimum Tm at about 30% DL (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DSC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 70% DL, the membrane is about 6 Å thinner than that with no DL.
source: Using a spherical, multi-lamellar liposome model to fit the scattering spectra (Figure 3D,E), we observe a gradual decrease in the bilayer thickness as the DL content is increased (Figure 3F); at 70% DL, the membrane is about 6 Å thinner than that with no DL.
evidence: This claim is supported by SANS measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The change in bilayer thickness with DL content is consistent with published SANS measurements for POPC vs. DLPC.
source: This change is consistent with published SANS measurements for POPC vs. DLPC (Kučerka et al., 2011) and POPG vs. DLPG (Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kučerka et al., 2011 and Pan et al., 2014.

claim: The change in bilayer thickness approximately matches the magnitude of the defect created by the CLC-ec1 monomer.
source: It also approximately matches the magnitude of the defect created by the CLC-ec1 monomer (Figure 2C), indicating that the DL lipids in these mixtures might be suitable for solvating the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing SANS data with simulation results.

claim: As DL is added to PO membranes, their lipid headgroups remain aligned with those of the PO lipids.
source: Further analysis indicates a high degree of cooperativity between the two lipid-chain types: for example, if the bilayer thickness is quantified by the distance between the two ester layers, there is virtually no difference when this distance is evaluated only for DL vs. PO lipids, at any % DL (Figure 3G). This observation indicates that as DL is added, their lipid headgroups remain aligned with those of the PO lipids so as to minimally perturb the degree of hydration of the headgroup layer.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The average number of contacts formed between the acyl chains in one leaflet and those in the other is a conserved quantity, regardless of the PO/DL content.
source: It is worth noting that the average number of contacts formed between the acyl chains in one leaflet and those in the other is also a conserved quantity, regardless of the PO/DL content (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: A given DL chain can form only half of the interleaflet contacts seen for the PO chains in the absence of DL.
source: For example, comparing the 0% and 10% DL membranes, we observe that a given DL chain can form only half of the interleaflet contacts seen for the PO chains in the absence of DL.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis.

claim: The site-specific labeling procedure provides a consistent labeling yield, PCy5,WT = 0.663 ± 0.005.
source: Our site-specific labeling procedure (Chadda et al., 2016; Chadda and Robertson, 2016) provides a consistent labeling yield, PCy5,WT = 0.663 ± 0.005 (mean ± sem, n = 27 independent purifications with Cy5 labeling, Figure 4—source data 7); thus, as long as we know the liposome size distribution, we can determine any changes of CLC-ec1 dimerization equilibrium in different lipid environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 27 independent purifications.

claim: 2:1 PE/PG membranes containing 20% DL and 80% PO appear similar to those in the 0% DL condition.
source: The liposomes and membranes appear similar to those in the 0% DL condition (i.e. 2:1 POPE/POPG), with comparable radius and fractional surface area distributions (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM imaging data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: There is a significant proportion of multilamellar vesicles in both 20% DL (44%) and 100% PO (25%) samples.
source: There is a significant proportion of multilamellar vesicles in both compositions, 44% for 20% DL and 25% for 100% PO samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM imaging analysis.

claim: The 20% DL condition destabilizes CLC-ec1 dimerization by at least +3 kcal/mole.
source: Still, the limited reaction indicates that the 20% DL condition destabilizes dimerization by at least +3 kcal/mole.
evidence: This claim is supported by photobleaching analysis and fitting to dimerization isotherms.

claim: CLC-ec1 remained effective at transporting chloride in 20% DL.
source: The protein remained effective at transporting chloride in 20% DL (Figure 4I), with no difference in the fraction of inactive vesicles (Figure 4J), and a modest twofold decrease in chloride efflux rate (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by chloride efflux measurements shown in Figures 4I, 4J, and 4K.

claim: There is no difference in the fraction of inactive vesicles between 0% and 20% DL.
source: The protein remained effective at transporting chloride in 20% DL (Figure 4I), with no difference in the fraction of inactive vesicles (Figure 4J), and a modest twofold decrease in chloride efflux rate (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional measurements shown in Figure 4J.

claim: There is a modest twofold decrease in chloride efflux rate in 20% DL compared to 0% DL.
source: The protein remained effective at transporting chloride in 20% DL (Figure 4I), with no difference in the fraction of inactive vesicles (Figure 4J), and a modest twofold decrease in chloride efflux rate (Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional measurements shown in Figure 4K.

claim: CLC-ec1 is significantly destabilized toward the dissociated monomeric form in 20% DL, 80% PO 2:1 PE/PG membranes, yet remains a functionally competent chloride transporter.
source: Therefore, CLC-ec1 is significantly destabilized toward the dissociated monomeric form in 20% DL, 80% PO 2:1 PE/PG membranes, yet remains a functionally competent chloride transporter in the new lipid composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by both photobleaching and functional data.

claim: The impact of DL on dimerization follows two phases with an inflection point around 1% DL.
source: Calculation of Fdimer from these data shows that the impact of DL on dimerization follows two phases with an inflection point around 1% DL (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of photobleaching data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For samples with 10% DL or less, there is no change in chloride transport activity.
source: For samples with 10% DL or less, we observed no change in chloride transport activity; by contrast, at 40% DL there is approximately a 70% reduction in transport rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by chloride transport measurements.

claim: At 40% DL there is approximately a 70% reduction in transport rate.
source: For samples with 10% DL or less, we observed no change in chloride transport activity; by contrast, at 40% DL there is approximately a 70% reduction in transport rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by chloride transport measurements.

claim: Greater than 60% of the dimerization changes occur below 10% DL, before there are any major changes in the macroscopic structure of the membrane.
source: From this plot, we can see that > 60% of the dimerization changes occur below 10% DL, that is, before there are any major changes in the macroscopic structure of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of dimerization and SANS data.

claim: The change in chloride efflux rate correlates directly with the change in bilayer thickness.
source: However, the change in chloride efflux rate correlates directly with the change in bilayer thickness.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of functional and SANS data.

claim: At DL >1%, the complex is destabilized by 0.8 ± 0.3 kcal/mole for every addition of 10% DL in the membrane.
source: At DL >1%, the complex is destabilized by 0.8 ± 0.3 kcal/mole for every addition of 10% DL in the membrane (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of free energy changes shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At DL <1%, ΔΔG shows a linear dependency with the logarithm of DL, with a destabilization of 0.14 ± 0.07 kcal/mole for every Log10 change in % DL.
source: However, at DL <1%, ΔΔG shows a linear dependency with the logarithm of DL, with a destabilization of 0.14 ± 0.07 kcal/mole for every Log10 change in % DL (Figure 5E, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of free energy changes shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A linear dependency of ΔΔG on the logarithm of the co-solvent activity corresponds to a thermodynamic linkage model of preferential solvation.
source: It also indicates the molecular mechanism, as a linear dependency of ΔΔG on the logarithm of the co-solvent activity corresponds to a thermodynamic linkage model of preferential solvation, as described by Tanford, 1969; Record and Anderson, 1995; Marsh, 1995; Timasheff, 2002a.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established thermodynamic theory.

claim: The thinned-membrane defect around the dimerization interface is still observed in the mixed PO/DL simulations, even for 50% DL.
source: Interestingly, the thinned-membrane defect around the dimerization interface is still observed in the mixed PO/DL simulations, even for 50% DL (Figure 6A), and is comparable to what we find in the 2:1 POPE/POPG simulations (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For 50% DL, the thinning defect is about 5.5 Å.
source: That is, the defect is observed even when the 'macroscopic' thickness of the lipid bilayer is reduced; for example, for 50% DL, the thinning is about 5.5 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis.

claim: Both PO and DL lipids solvate the totality of the protein surface.
source: Examination of the average lipid structure across the membrane show that both PO and DL lipids solvate the totality of the protein surface and that, as in the 100% PO condition, the thinned-membrane defect results from both types of lipids becoming increasingly tilted as they approach the dimerization interface (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DL lipids are not distributed identically to PO lipids at the protein surface.
source: However, 3D density maps for the first lipid solvation shell indicate these two lipid types are not distributed identically (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D density maps shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DL chains are too short to solvate the hydrophobic span of the protein at the two interfaces not involved in dimerization.
source: At the two interfaces not involved in dimerization, the DL density signal weakens at the center of the membrane, revealing the DL chains are too short to solvate the hydrophobic span of the protein, which is better matched to PO lipids.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of 3D density maps.

claim: PO is depleted at the dimerization interface in mixed PO/DL membranes.
source: Conversely, the density signal for PO is weaker than DL at the dimerization interface, and weaker than that seen in the 100% PO membrane, indicating PO is depleted here.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of 3D density maps.

claim: DL lipids are enriched at the dimerization interface.
source: This depletion, and the corresponding enrichment in DL lipids, becomes apparent in 2D projections of the percent difference between the observed lipid density ratio (DL/PO) and the expected bulk ratio (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The normalized probability of observing DL rather than PO at the dimerization interface is higher than elsewhere in the membrane, irrespective of PO/DL composition.
source: These data show that the normalized probability of observing DL rather than PO at the dimerization interface is higher than elsewhere in the membrane, irrespective of PO/DL composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid density ratios.

claim: DL is depleted at the other two interfaces (not involved in dimerization).
source: Conversely, DL is depleted at the other two interfaces, consistent with the 3D density analysis discussed above.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of lipid density ratios.

claim: The DL enrichment extends for up to 30 Å from the dimerization interface.
source: Quantification of the DL enrichment as a function of the distance from the protein surface reveals this effect extends for up to 30 Å from the dimerization interface and confirms that it is largely independent of the PO/DL ratio (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The DL enrichment is largely independent of the PO/DL ratio.
source: Quantification of the DL enrichment as a function of the distance from the protein surface reveals this effect extends for up to 30 Å from the dimerization interface and confirms that it is largely independent of the PO/DL ratio (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The enrichment effect is discernable at 1% DL, in conditions where there is virtually no change in the global thickness of the bilayer.
source: It is important to note, however, that the enrichment effect we report is discernable at 1% DL, that is, in conditions where there is virtually no change in the global thickness of the bilayer, relative to the PO condition, both in experiment and simulation (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data.

claim: 1% DL has a profound impact on the dimerization equilibrium.
source: Yet, 1% DL has a profound impact on the dimerization equilibrium (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by photobleaching data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Each lipid, on average, is in direct contact with 80% of all other lipids in the course of each simulation.
source: In our case, this analysis shows that each lipid, on average, is in direct contact with 80% of all other lipids in the course of each of our simulations (i.e. over 1100 molecules) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The enrichment of DL at the dimerization interface is neither artifactual nor transient but rather a minimum free-energy state of the lipid-solvent structure.
source: The observation of near complete lipid mixing in our simulations implies that the enrichment of DL at the dimerization interface is neither artifactual nor transient but rather a minimum free-energy state of the lipid-solvent structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of extensive lipid mixing in simulations.

claim: In the bulk membrane, there is no difference in the number of interleaflet contacts between the 100% PO and 50/50 PO/DL conditions when all lipids are averaged.
source: In the bulk, there is no difference between the 100% and 50/50 PO/DL conditions, for example, when all lipids are averaged.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of interleaflet contacts from simulations.

claim: At the CLC-ec1 dimerization interface, PO lipids create an excessive, clearly non-native overlap between leaflets.
source: At the CLC-ec1 dimerization interface, however, this conserved quantity cannot be matched by the PO lipids; whether for 100% PO or 50/50 PO/DL, PO lipids create an excessive, clearly non-native overlap between leaflets.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of interleaflet contacts shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When at the dimerization interface, DL chains very closely reproduce the conserved bulk values of interleaflet contacts.
source: By contrast, when at the dimerization interface, DL chains very closely reproduce the conserved bulk values.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of interleaflet contacts shown in Figure 7A.

claim: By segregating PO lipids away from the dimerization interface and accumulating DL lipids instead, the system minimizes the negative impact of the thinned-membrane defect created by the CLC monomer.
source: Thus, by segregating PO lipids away from this interface, and accumulating DL lipids instead, the system minimizes the negative impact of the thinned-membrane defect created by the CLC monomer, shifting the equilibrium toward the dissociated state.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of interleaflet contacts and lipid distribution.

claim: In 100% PO the CLC monomer introduces a clear lipid-density defect at the dimerization interface, particularly at the level of the headgroup and ester-linkage layers.
source: The data shows that in 100% PO the CLC monomer introduces a clear lipid-density defect at the dimerization interface, particularly at the level of the headgroup and ester-linkage layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The lipid-density defect leads to a marked increase in the degree of water penetration of the hydrocarbon interior of the bilayer, by almost threefold relative to the bulk-membrane values.
source: This perturbation, in turn, leads to a marked increase in the degree of water penetration of the hydrocarbon interior of the bilayer, by almost threefold relative to the bulk-membrane values (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The preferential solvation of the dimerization interface by DL does not entirely eradicate the membrane defects, but greatly minimizes them.
source: The preferential solvation of the dimerization interface by DL does not entirely eradicate these defects, but it is clear from our data that they are greatly minimized (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figures 7B and 7C.

claim: In the PO/DL conditions the energetic cost of lipid solvation of the monomer is reduced, relative to the pure PO condition.
source: In view of these results, we can plausibly infer that in the PO/DL conditions the energetic cost of lipid solvation of the monomer is reduced, relative to the pure PO condition.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing reduced membrane defects with DL.

claim: The dimerization of CLC-ec1 can be driven in large part by the energetic cost of lipid solvation of the monomeric state.
source: This study demonstrates that the dimerization of a membrane protein can be driven in large part by the energetic cost of lipid solvation of the monomeric state, due to the exposure of a protein surface that deforms the membrane structure.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both experimental and computational data.

claim: The monomer-dimer free-energy balance can be modulated by a mechanism of preferential solvation.
source: In our studies, we observe that the monomer-dimer free-energy balance can be modulated by a mechanism of preferential solvation, that is, the enrichment of specific lipid types that are more naturally predisposed to reside in the membrane defect caused by the dissociated protomers.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study, supported by experimental and computational data.

claim: Preferential solvation occurs with low quantities of the modulatory lipid in the membrane, before macroscopic changes in membrane thickness are apparent.
source: This is an effect that occurs with low quantities of the modulatory lipid in the membrane, before macroscopic changes in membrane thickness are apparent, and where the functionality of the protein is preserved.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects at 1% DL.

claim: When global changes in membrane thickness become significant, the dimerization equilibrium has already shifted drastically, and the physical state of the membrane is observed to degrade protein function.
source: In contrast, when global changes in membrane thickness become significant, the dimerization equilibrium has already shifted drastically, and the physical state of the membrane is observed to degrade protein function.
evidence: This is supported by functional data at high DL concentrations.

claim: Preferential solvation is a plausible contender for a mechanism of physiological regulation of membrane protein complexes in biological membranes.
source: Thus, we find that preferential solvation is a plausible contender for a mechanism of physiological regulation of membrane protein complexes in biological membranes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The free energy of CLC-ec1 dimerization in 2:1 POPE/POPG lipid bilayers is −10.9 ± 0.1 kcal/mole.
source: Experimentally, we have measured that the free energy of CLC-ec1 dimerization in 2:1 POPE/POPG lipid bilayers is −10.9 ± 0.1 kcal/mole (one subunit/lipid standard state).
evidence: This is an experimental measurement from previous work.

claim: It is very likely that the CLC-ec1 dimerization reaction is driven largely by the energetics of the membrane, with protein-protein interactions contributing on a smaller scale.
source: Given the nature of the perturbations caused by the monomer, and the fact that this free-energy value can be drastically shifted by addition of minimal amounts of DLPE/DLPG lipids, we believe it is very likely that this dimerization reaction is driven largely by the energetics of the membrane, with protein-protein interactions contributing on a smaller scale.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental and computational findings.

claim: Membrane protein complexes may evolve high shape-complementarity to maximize the exclusion of lipids in the complexed form of the protein.
source: Membrane protein complexes may thus evolve high shape-complementarity, for example to maximize the exclusion of lipids in the complexed form of the protein (Li et al., 2013), and thereby achieve greater stability.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings, supported by a citation to Li et al., 2013.

claim: CLC-ec1 exhibits high shape-complementarity, comparable to other high-affinity antigen antibody complexes.
source: Indeed, previous analysis showed that CLC-ec1 exhibits high shape-complementarity, comparable to other high-affinity antigen antibody complexes (Robertson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robertson et al., 2010.

claim: Assembly of Gramicidin A peptides into functional ion-channel dimers results in a hydrophobic mismatch with the surrounding bilayer.
source: Assembly of Gramicidin A peptides into functional ion-channel dimers results in a hydrophobic mismatch with the surrounding bilayer, and thus dimerization can be inhibited by increasing the global membrane thickness (Goodall, 1971; Mobashery et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goodall, 1971 and Mobashery et al., 1997.

claim: Dimerization of Gramicidin A can be inhibited by increasing the global membrane thickness.
source: Assembly of Gramicidin A peptides into functional ion-channel dimers results in a hydrophobic mismatch with the surrounding bilayer, and thus dimerization can be inhibited by increasing the global membrane thickness (Goodall, 1971; Mobashery et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goodall, 1971 and Mobashery et al., 1997.

claim: FRET measurements for reconstituted Rhodopsin have indicated the formation of higher order assemblies when the membrane is thicker or thinner than a certain range.
source: FRET measurements for reconstituted Rhodopsin have indicated the formation of higher order assemblies when the membrane is thicker or thinner than a certain range (Botelho et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Botelho et al., 2006.

claim: ATP synthases in the inner mitochondrial membranes spontaneously assemble into micrometer-scale linear arrays, priming the membrane to invaginate and form cristae.
source: A striking illustration of this concept is found in the inner mitochondrial membranes, where ATP synthases, each a dimeric complex, spontaneously assemble into micrometer-scale linear arrays, priming the membrane to invaginate and form cristae (Anselmi et al., 2018, Blum et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anselmi et al., 2018 and Blum et al., 2019.

claim: There is a growing body of evidence that suggests that membrane-dependent forces are a key factor in the self-assembly and organization of membrane protein complexes.
source: Thus, there is a growing body of evidence that suggests that membrane-dependent forces are a key factor in the self-assembly and organization of membrane protein complexes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on cited literature.

claim: This study is the first to probe how membrane-dependent forces can dictate the oligomerization equilibrium of a strongly-bound integral membrane protein complex, in the absence of global physical membrane changes, and without compromising its biological functionality.
source: To our knowledge, however, this study is the first to probe how such forces can dictate the oligomerization equilibrium of a strongly-bound integral membrane protein complex, in the absence of global physical membrane changes, and without compromising its biological functionality.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The gradual, linear relationship of the decay of the dimeric population with the logarithm of % DL over six orders of magnitude is not in agreement with a model of site-specific competitive binding.
source: The gradual, linear relationship of the decay of the dimeric population with the logarithm of % DL that we observe in our data, over six orders of magnitude, is simply not in agreement with a model of site-specific competitive binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and thermodynamic theory.

claim: Preferential solvation effects alone can dictate the energetics of oligomerization reactions for integral membrane proteins.
source: The experiments and simulations described in our study indeed confirm that preferential solvation effects alone can dictate the energetics of oligomerization reactions for integral membrane proteins, even those that are assumed to be obligate oligomers, where the associated form appears to be derived from evolutionarily pressures, for example CLC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and computational findings.

claim: The enrichment of DL lipids at the dimerization interface is specific to the monomeric state that exposes this interface.
source: This enrichment is specific to the dimerization interface, and therefore also specific for the monomeric state that exposes this interface.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation data showing DL enrichment only at the exposed dimerization interface.

claim: The enrichment of DL lipids is observed irrespective of the PO/DL content of the bilayer.
source: And importantly, it is observed irrespective of the PO/DL content of the bilayer, as could be expected for an effect that is dictated by the protein itself.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data at different DL concentrations.

claim: Preferential solvation would appear to be a more viable mechanism of lipid regulation of oligomerization reactions of specific species under physiological conditions where biology strives to maintain global membrane properties.
source: Preferential solvation would thus appear to be a more viable mechanism of lipid regulation of oligomerization reactions of specific species under physiological conditions where biology strives to maintain global membrane properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and physiological considerations.

claim: Preferential solvation is a generalizable effect that could modulate any equilibrium whereby one or more protein states introduce a local morphological defect into the membrane.
source: Preferential solvation is a generalizable effect that could modulate any equilibrium whereby one or more protein states introduce a local morphological defect into the membrane.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Each conformational state of a membrane protein will have a different local lipid composition, optimized to stabilize the structure of the membrane in that state.
source: Given the highly complex composition of real biological membranes, one can therefore envisage that each of these conformational states will have a different local lipid composition, optimized to stabilize the structure of the membrane in that state.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: It is rare for a membrane to change its composition so much that its macroscopic structure is significantly altered.
source: Cell membranes are known to undergo changes in lipid composition due to many external factors (Marr and Ingraham, 1962; Sanders and Mittendorf, 2011); yet, it is rare for a membrane to change its composition so much that its macroscopic structure is significantly altered.
evidence: This is a statement about biological membranes supported by citations.

claim: The membranes of E. coli cells grown at colder temperatures will primarily decrease chain saturation, with only minor changes to the amount of short-chain lipids.
source: For instance, the membranes of E. coli cells grown at colder temperatures will primarily decrease chain saturation, with only minor changes to the amount of short-chain lipids.
evidence: This is a statement about E. coli membrane adaptation.

claim: There is no situation where a cell will change the overall macroscopic thickness of its membranes due to a physiological stimulus.
source: As far as we know, there is no situation where a cell will change the overall macroscopic thickness of its membranes due to a physiological stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about biological membrane homeostasis.

claim: CLC-ec1 dimerization is sensitive to the amount of the short-chain DL lipid in the membrane even at low levels, from 10−8 to 1%.
source: Our experiments show that CLC-ec1 dimerization is sensitive to the amount of the short-chain DL lipid in the membrane; even at low levels, from 10−8 to 1%, we observe a gradual and non-saturating impact, indicating that dimerization is tunable without a global change in the state of the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental photobleaching data.

claim: The resulting change in the dimer population, from 80% to 50%, could certainly impart a physiological effect if it was linked to a cell signaling function.
source: The resulting change in the dimer population, from 80% to 50%, could certainly impart a physiological effect if it was linked to a cell signaling function.
evidence: This is a speculation about the physiological relevance of the findings.

claim: Preferential solvation naturally allows for gradual tuning of oligomerization equilibria.
source: It is equally important to note that the phenomenon of preferential solvation naturally allows for this gradual tuning, as opposed to what would be expected for a process of site-specific lipid-ligand binding, which would inhibit dimerization in a switch-like manner over a much narrower range of DL-lipid concentrations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and thermodynamic theory.

claim: DL lipids disproportionately accumulate at the membrane defect created by monomeric CLC-ec1.
source: In simulations, we observe the CLC-ec1 monomers force PO lipids to adopt non-native conformations, and many of the features of the bilayer near the dimerization interface, ranging from lipid tilt-angle to interleaflet contacts or water exclusion, are radically different from those in the bulk. When DL lipids are present, they disproportionately accumulate at this defect, spontaneously, while maintaining non-specific interactions.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data.

claim: DL lipids restore some of the bulk-like features to the bilayer near the dimerization interface.
source: In doing so, DL lipids restore some of the bulk-like features to the bilayer near the dimerization interface.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data.

claim: DL could be considered a chemical that drives disaggregation, analogous to chaotropic denaturants stabilizing the un-folded states of proteins in aqueous solution.
source: A small lipid like DL could thus be considered a chemical that drives disaggregation, analogous to chaotropic denaturants stabilizing the un-folded states of proteins in aqueous solution.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from the findings.

claim: Many regulatory molecules in membranes are small fatty acids.
source: Many regulatory molecules in membranes are also small fatty acids; pharmacological agents like general anesthetics are small non-polar molecules as well.
evidence: This is a statement about known regulatory molecules.

claim: Small lipoidal factors may act similarly to DL by preferentially solvating and stabilizing the membrane in states where local deformations and defects created by a protein become exposed.
source: It is possible that these small lipoidal factors act similarly to DL in the problem examined here, and that they preferentially solvate and stabilize the membrane in states where local deformations and defects created by a protein become exposed.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

claim: The complexity of lipid compositions found in biological cell membranes, leveraged through mechanisms such as preferential solvation, permits the cell to regulate and fine-tune the reactions of membrane proteins.
source: Altogether, our findings lead to the hypothesis that the complexity of lipid compositions found in biological cell membranes, leveraged through mechanisms such as preferential solvation, permits the cell to regulate and fine-tune the reactions of membrane proteins within – folding, oligomerization, and conformational changes – amidst the extremely variable conditions that life faces.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: All simulations were calculated with GROMACS 5.2.1 using the MARTINI 2.2/ElNeDyn22 forcefield.
source: All simulations were calculated with GROMACS 5.2.1 (Abraham et al., 2015) using the MARTINI 2.2/ElNeDyn22 forcefield (Wassenaar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the simulations.

claim: Temperature and pressure were maintained constant at 303.15 K and 1 bar in the simulations.
source: Temperature and pressure were maintained constant at 303.15 K and 1 bar, using the velocity-rescale thermostat and the Parrinello-Rahman semi-isotropic barostat, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the simulations.

claim: The simulations are based on the crystal structure of wild-type CLC-ec1 dimer deposited in the Protein Data Bank, entry 1OTS.
source: The simulations are based on the crystal structure of wild-type CLC-ec1 dimer deposited in the Protein Data Bank, entry 1OTS (resolution 2.51 Å) (Dutzler et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the simulations.

claim: Chloride ions were included at sites Scen and Sint in the simulations.
source: Chloride ions were included at sites Scen and Sint, and E113 (chains A and B) and D417 (chain A) were protonated as indicated from electrostatics analysis (Faraldo-Gómez and Roux, 2004)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the simulations.

claim: In the monomer state the N-terminus was truncated up to residue 30.
source: In the monomer state the N-terminus was truncated up to residue 30, as this cytoplasmic helix, which domain-swaps in the dimer, is highly flexible and able to adopt alternate conformations (Robertson et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the simulations.
